drafts.angle: Bad reply rates are usually a list problem, not a copy problem — the prospect file deserves the same scrutiny as the message.

linkedin.content:
When a cold campaign underperforms, the instinct is to rewrite the opening line. Usually that's the wrong fix.

The Expandi Blog has a solid primer on building prospect lists that's worth a read: https://expandi.io/blog/how-to-build-a-prospect-list/. The point that stands out most to us: a lead list isn't just a column of names and emails — it should record *why* each person belongs there and how closely they match your ICP. Without that, you're essentially A/B testing copy on the wrong audience.

In practice, we see this constantly. A sequence gets blamed for low reply rates, the team iterates on subject lines for two weeks, and the underlying issue is that half the list never fit the ICP to begin with. Tightening the list — even by 30% — often moves reply rates more than any messaging tweak.

Before your next campaign refresh, it's worth asking: when did you last audit the list itself, not just the copy?

drafts.angle: A seven-step checklist is a fine starting point, but the gap between 'following steps' and actually booking meetings lives in the judgment calls the checklist can't capture.

linkedin.content:
Most cold email guides give you a process. The harder part is the discretion inside the process.

Instantly Blog published a solid seven-step breakdown covering prospect sourcing, verification, personalisation, and follow-up sequencing (https://instantly.ai/blog/how-to-generate-leads-using-cold-email/). Worth a read if you're building or auditing a cold email motion.

What the checklist format can't show you: when to cut a sequence short because the signal isn't there, how to tell the difference between a deliverability problem and a positioning problem, or why the same message structure works for one ICP and flatlines for another. That's where most teams lose time — running the steps correctly but tuning the wrong variables.

The mechanics of cold email are increasingly accessible. The thinking that goes into who you target, what you say, and what you do with the data you get back — that part still requires someone paying close attention.
